report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to generate news-style headlines/captions (summaries in a headline register), i.e., short, punchy, often sensational, “headliney” continuations of text.

Reasoning:
- Strong first-token shift: The difference norm is overwhelmingly concentrated at position 0 across almost all layers (peaking massively at L25 p0), which is typical of a finetune that imposes a fixed “opening style” or format—here, a headline/caption lead.
- Headline lexical markers: Across mid-to-late layers, top tokens repeatedly include “headline(s)”, “BY” (byline marker), proper names and roles common in news (“Driver”, “Sessions”, “Vincent”, “Hunter”), event/news nouns and verbs (“visits”, “nearing”, “coming”, “port”, “hurricane”, “victims”, “refugees”, “law”, “film”).
- Headline/caption adjectives: Positions 2–4 at layers 19–25 are dominated by a stereotypical headline/culture-journalism adjective set: “iconic”, “tragic”, “timeless”, “vivid”, “colorful”, “vibrant”, “lush”, “loud”, “furry”, “melodic”, plus “moments”, “names”, “podcast”. This cluster is characteristic of news/culture captions, photo galleries, and arts/entertainment headlines.
- Sensational framing: Frequent “worst”, “blitz”, “refused”, “shocked”, “alert”, “major”, “strive/optimize” (punchy, imperative/telegraphic tone) matches headline register.
- Numbers early on (e.g., “6 8 7 9 5 1”) suggest listicle/headline patterns (“5 ways…”, “7 things…”), common in newsy/clickbait titling.

Together these point to a finetune that steers outputs toward condensed, capitalized/punchy news headlines or captions rather than general prose.
